title: The potato trade that looked profitable but wasn't
summary: Agra → Vashi New Mumbai, January 2025: a ₹390 per quintal median price gap on 31 matched days. After modeled costs: −₹43 per quintal on the typical day.
why_selected: Chosen automatically for January 2025: one of AGRINET's documented trade corridors with 31 matched report days.

evidence.observations: daily modal prices; sale matched to the first destination report 1–3 days after transit
caveats: Hypothetical: no actual shipment is claimed.

scenes.headline: January 2025
scenes.caption: Agra sits in western Uttar Pradesh's cold-stored potato belt; Vashi supplies Mumbai.

scenes.headline: Two markets, two prices
scenes.caption: On 31 matched days, Agra reported a median ₹1,270 per quintal; Vashi New Mumbai reported ₹1,650 2 days later.

scenes.headline: Gap ₹390/qtl
scenes.caption: The median gross gap was ₹390 per quintal and was positive on 100% of days.

scenes.headline: 1,270 km by road
scenes.caption: Routed road distance 1,270 km (OpenStreetMap car routing, ~15 driving hours). Trucks are slower; we allow 2 days.

scenes.headline: Now add the costs
scenes.caption: Freight ≈₹273/qtl, 5% fees and commission, loading, 5% loss and interest. Modeled net on the typical (median) day: −₹43 per quintal.

scenes.headline: Stress test
scenes.caption: With 25% dearer freight, 10% loss and costlier credit, the typical day becomes −₹199 per quintal.

scenes.headline: Hindsight vs. a real trader
scenes.caption: With perfect hindsight, 9 of 31 days cleared modeled costs. A trader using only reports available on the day would have shipped on 11 of 31 days, averaging −₹34 per quintal; 7 of those shipments lost money.

scenes.headline: The lesson
scenes.caption: The ₹390 gap looked tempting, but on the typical day modeled costs absorbed it. A gap on a price board is not a margin.

assumptions.value: scaled by road km against the 1,115 km Lasalgaon→Azadpur route → ₹273/qtl here
12% a year (14% adverse) for transit + 7 days

conclusion: The ₹390 gap looked tempting, but on the typical day modeled costs absorbed it. A gap on a price board is not a margin.

title: Why storing potatoes is complicated
summary: Agra potatoes: ₹1,100 in March 2025, ₹1,090 in October. Break-even storage budget: ₹-163 per quintal.
why_selected: Chosen automatically: the yearly harvest-to-autumn storage question at Agra, with 11 earlier seasons to learn from.

evidence.observations: monthly medians of Agra daily modal prices (≥8 reports)
caveats: No cold-storage rent is cited, so no net profit is claimed.
Stored and fresh potatoes may differ in grade.

scenes.headline: March 2025
scenes.caption: Potatoes are harvested in early spring and often held in cold stores in western Uttar Pradesh, which the RBI paper calls the potato belt's key selling point.

scenes.headline: Harvest price
scenes.caption: Agra's March 2025 median: ₹1,100 per quintal.

scenes.headline: The informed bet
scenes.caption: Using only the 11 earlier years, March→October had averaged +₹429. A rule-following trader would store.

scenes.headline: October 2025
scenes.caption: October median: ₹1,090, a change of -0.9%.

scenes.headline: Shrinkage and interest
scenes.caption: Allowing 7% loss and 12% a year interest for 7 months leaves a storage budget of ₹-163 per quintal.

scenes.headline: The lesson
scenes.caption: Even before paying any storage rent, shrinkage and interest wiped out the gain: holding lost about ₹163 per quintal.

assumptions.value: not in cited evidence; shown as break-even budget

conclusion: Even before paying any storage rent, shrinkage and interest wiped out the gain: holding lost about ₹163 per quintal.
